title: Heatwave Week
briefing: Day 1 of a five-day heatwave: 38C forecast. Two compressors at Corby Road are running at their limit, a third site reports rising store temperatures, and three pharma loads are due out tonight.
The COO is abroad. You are the most senior risk person on site and the crisis team is looking at you.

context.text: Automated temperature alerting from Coldline 2 is live at four sites: you can see every store in real time.
Contractor sign-off records show Corby Road's compressors were serviced last month.
The crisis playbook from your stress-test work names decision owners for exactly this.

evidence.title: Store temperatures (live)
evidence.body: Corby Road chilled: 6.8C rising 0.3C/hour (limit 8C). Eastfield: 5.1C stable. Northgate: 4.2C stable. Harrowgate: 7.4C, door seal damaged.

evidence.title: Tonight's pharma loads
evidence.body: Three loads, value 1.1m, from Corby Road. Client contract: product above 8C for more than 30 minutes must be quarantined and reported.

evidence.title: Resources
evidence.body: Two hired mobile cold units available within 4 hours (8,000 a day each). Spare capacity at Northgate for about 40% of Corby Road's stock. Kelvarin's emergency line answers.

questions.prompt: What do you do in the first hour?

options.label: Hire both mobile units, start moving high-value pharma stock to Northgate, call Kelvarin to Corby Road, and get Harrowgate's door seal fixed or the store closed
options.feedback: Acts on the store about to breach, protects the most valuable stock, and contains the second site.

options.label: Wait for the COO to call back before spending money
options.feedback: At 0.3C an hour, Corby Road breaches in about four hours.

schedules.description: Corby Road chilled store passes 8C overnight; stock quarantined

options.label: Ship the pharma loads early, before temperatures rise further
options.feedback: Moves the problem onto the road without fixing the store, and the loads may not be ready.

questions.prompt: What do you tell the pharma client?

options.label: Call now: the situation, what you're doing, temperature logs for their loads, and when you'll update next
options.feedback: Clients forgive problems; they don't forgive surprises.

options.label: Tell them afterwards if anything went wrong
options.feedback: If the contract reporting rule is breached, late disclosure compounds it.

options.label: Tell them everything is fine
options.feedback: Untrue, and logged data will show it.

questions.prompt: How do you organise the crisis team?

options.label: One incident lead (you), named owners for stock moves, engineering and client contact, a two-hour update rhythm, and a decision log
options.feedback: Clear roles and rhythm prevent duplicated and dropped tasks.

options.label: Do the critical tasks yourself
options.feedback: The leader's job is to coordinate, not to drive the forklift.

questions.prompt: The response will cost about 50,000 a day for up to five days. Your authority is 750,000. What governance applies?

options.label: Within your authority: spend, log each decision and its rationale, and inform the COO and CFO with a cost forecast
options.feedback: Use your authority, and keep the record that makes it accountable.

options.label: Seek approval for each hire
options.feedback: Wastes hours you don't have; the authority exists for this.

options.label: Spend what's needed and sort the paperwork later
options.feedback: Decisions without a record are hard to defend later.

questions.prompt: After the heatwave, what do you take to the executive?

options.label: A blameless after-action review: what worked, what failed, cost, and three changes (e.g. pre-contracted mobile units, heat-trigger thresholds, door-seal checks)
options.feedback: Turns the crisis into lasting resilience without a witch-hunt.

options.label: A thank-you note to the team
A report on who caused the problems

lesson: In a crisis: act on the fastest-moving risk first, organise roles and rhythm, use your authority and log it, tell clients early, and learn without blame.
